title: Version Control, Change Review and Effective Dates

content.overview: Controlled procedures need stable versions. A change should preserve what changed, why, who approved it, when it becomes effective and which training or records are affected, while superseded versions remain retrievable for historical investigation.

vocabulary.definition: Date from which an approved controlled document is intended to govern work.
A prior version replaced by a newer approved version but retained as historical evidence.
Evaluation of people, records, training, systems or dependent procedures affected by a revision.

sections.title: Do not edit history in place
sections.body: Published or effective procedures should be revised through a new version rather than silently changing the prior record.

sections.title: Review dependencies before release
sections.body: A changed procedure can affect forms, training, equipment settings, assessment items or downstream SOPs.

sections.title: Effective date creates an operational boundary
sections.body: Approval, training and implementation need to align so staff are not simultaneously working from conflicting versions.

workedExamples: Changing a sampling location may require a new form diagram and training update, not just one sentence in the SOP.
A deviation investigation from last year must be able to retrieve the SOP version that was effective at that time.
commonMistakes: Releasing a version before impacted roles can access or train on it.
content.practicalApplication: For a sample revision, document old/new version, change summary, reason, approver, impacted documents/roles, required training and effective date.
content.summary: Version control keeps current work consistent while preserving historical evidence needed for review and investigation.
